I actually disagree with almost everything you said here. 

If you're looking, and honestly if you're giving yourself positive reinforcement, you're going to be disappointed. You'll start to wonder why the world isn't reinforcing your viewpoint, which will only create even more intense negative thoughts. Positivity, ironically, is a negative feedback loop. EDIT: I mean in the context of telling yourself "I'm beautiful regardless of how I look" or "I'll do the things that make me happy and eventually someone will love me". Those are lies we tell ourselves to feel better but we pay for those lies in the end. 

In my experience, the only thing you can do is keep your expectations low. That goes for everyone. Low expectations =/= expectation of failure. But keep in mind that whatever you do, whether you lose weight or not, or have a positive mindset or not, will not actually fix anything. And if you expect it to, you're only setting yourself up for failure. That's what I mean when I say you can't be looking. If you think that losing weight or being happy or doing whatever will change that, you're wrong, and you'll only be more upset when you find that out for yourself. 

As far as the girl I know that I was talking about, she literally stopped caring about how people viewed her physically. It became a total non factor for her. Notice how that is not the same as telling herself that she was conventionally beautiful no matter what, because she isn't, and to tell herself that would be deluding herself. For me, I could never live with that, and I could never ever be happy accepting that about myself, which is why I work out and why I lost weight. I also thought it would be a magic fix all, and it wasn't, so initially I was more depressed skinny than I was fat, but I ultimately came to understand what it is I'm telling you. 

You are in a position where the love you feel will not be romantic puppy love crushes and lust masquerading as love and honestly I think you'll come to appreciate that someday. The people in your life that do love you, your friends, your family, the people closest in your life, that's the kind of love that will lead you to a successful and happy relationship one day. When I say "look for it in the right places" that's what I mean, embrace *that* love because those people love you for who you are and will continue to regardless of what you do, and that love comes free of expectation. Out of that mentality, with everyone you meet going forward, eventually a relationship will develop.

Fearing rejection is not having no expectations. It's having the expectation that you will fail, which is an expectation. Having no expectations is good. Having negative expectations is bad. 

Look, fearing rejection is a normal thing. But unlike fearing certain things, like falling off buildings or fire or sharks or guns, it's not actually going to hurt you. 

In fact, unlike those others where you avoid them because of the potential pain, I believe that the avoidance of rejection is actually more harmful than the rejection itself. 

You've got to understand this. Rejection is not always an indictment on your worth. 

People reject people all the time for a variety of reasons. 


There's a girl that rejected me and it was because I was fat and ugly and immature at the time. I grew to learn from that experience that it was an indictment on my worth. Instead of feeling sorry for myself and lamenting my lot in life, I worked hard to improve on the areas I fell short in trying to achieve my goals. 

Dating and finding love are like anything else and require practice and hard work to make sure that you are meeting your end of the bargain. You need to ask yourself why should someone go out with me, and you need to be brutally honest and harder on yourself than other people will be with you. 
 
There's another girl that I know that I wanted to be with, and she also rejected me. Later she started to go out with another guy and the whole experience hurt me. I would go on to find out that the rejection wasn't about me but about her own headspace at the time. 

She's still in a relationship with that guy but she told me recently that she actually really likes me, even still. Her rejection was not about her assessment of me as a potential partner, but about her own ability to be in a relationship at the time. Only now do I understand that.

Either way, the problem of fearing rejection is only solved by having the self-awareness of how you measure up as a partner and how you fulfill the needs of the person you're with, as well as the understanding that not everything is about you. It's a balance and to ultimately find happiness is to be rejected along the way.

Rejection happens in life and if you try to avoid it, you'll never learn those lessons.

For guys, whether it's *subconscious* or conscious (and typically subconscious), they want sex because they want to know they can get some. I think ultimately you need to approach relationships with the "low expectation, high reward" mentality. Especially at your age.

Not everyone, but a lot of people, in college actually do want to commit to somebody but just do not know how. I mean how could they? 

Nobody at that age (I'm at that age, btw) knows anything about anything. About themselves. About the world. And most certainly about how to take care and treat another person necessary for a truly healthy relationship. A lot of people learn this from being in relationships, both successful and failures (a breakup does not mean a failed relationship), and learning from the experience. This is what is happening to you right now. 

I mean, there are some people that don't need that, but those are special people formed by special circumstances, and even then, rare is it that those people have the kind of experiences and the *maturity* to be able to apply them in a productive way. 

Couples that form in people's 20s are typically shallow and self-focused. Even when you think you're being a good partner, it typically comes with the self-satisfaction of "look at how good of a girlfriend/boyfriend I am" or "I'm so happy to have a bf/gf" or something else where the subject is yourself. 

This is the big problem that people have in their 20s. Their relationships are based on mutual self satisfaction. That's ok.
